blocks.html: SQL (Structured Query Language) es un lenguaje estándar utilizado para interactuar con bases de datos relacionales. Permite crear, modificar y consultar datos de manera eficiente. Esta cheatsheet está diseñada para ayudarte a aprender y recordar las instrucciones más comunes de SQL.

items: Query Basics: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE y WHERE.
Filtrado y orden: Operadores, ORDER BY, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, GROUP BY y HAVING.
Funciones: Funciones agregadas (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN), de cadena, numéricas y de fecha.
Tablas y Constraints: CREATE, ALTER, DROP TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT.
Índices y Auto Increment: Mejora el rendimiento de las consultas con índices y claves autoincrementales.

blocks.html: Puedes hacer clic en los siguientes enlaces para explorar cada sección:
The SELECT statement is used to select data from a database.
The data returned is stored in a result table, called the result-set.
Here, column1, column2, ... are the field names of the table you want to select data from. If you want to select all the fields available in the table, use the following syntax:
The following SQL statement selects the "first_name" and "last_name" columns from the "patients" table:
The following SQL statement selects all the columns from the "patients" table:
INSERT INTO statement is used to insert new records in a table.
It is possible to write the INSERT INTO statement in two ways:
1. Specify both the column names and the values to be inserted:

blocks.text: INSERT INTO tablename (column1, column2, column3, ...) VALUES (value1, value2, value3, ...);

blocks.html: 2. If you are adding values for all the columns of the table, you do not need to specify the column names in the SQL query. However, make sure the order of the values is in the same order as the columns in the table.

blocks.text: INSERT INTO tablename VALUES (value1, value2, value3, ...);

blocks.html: The following SQL statement inserts a new record in the patients table:

blocks.text: -- Insert a record INSERT INTO patients (first_name, last_name, gender, birth_date, city, province_id, allergies, weight, height) VALUES ('John', 'Smith', 'M', '1994-02-21', 'Hamilton', 'ON', NULL, 132, 182); -- Select the most recent record by id SELECT * FROM patients WHERE patient_id = (SELECT MAX(patient_id) FROM patients);
Insert Data Only in Specified Columns

blocks.html: It is also possible to only insert data in specific columns.
If the table column allow for NULL values then you do not need to include the column in your insert statement.

blocks.text: -- Insert a record INSERT INTO patients (first_name, last_name, gender) VALUES ('Jane', 'Doe', 'F'); -- Select the most recent record by id SELECT * FROM patients WHERE patient_id = (SELECT MAX(patient_id) FROM patients);

blocks.html: The DELETE statement is used to delete existing records in a table.
Note: Be sure to specify the where clause. Failing to include the where clause will result in all of the rows to be deleted.
The following SQL statement deletes all patients named "Paul" from the "patients" table:

blocks.text: DELETE FROM patients WHERE first_name = 'Paul'; -- There are no longer any patients named 'Paul' in the database SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name = 'Paul';

blocks.html: The UPDATE statement is used to modify the existing records in a table.

blocks.text: UPDATE tablename SET column1 = value1, column2 = value2, ... WHERE condition;

blocks.html: Note: Be sure to specify the where clause. Failing to include the where clause will result in all of the rows to be updated.
The following SQL statement updates the first patient (patient_id = 1) with a new first_name and a new weight.

blocks.text: UPDATE patients SET first_name = 'John', weight = 120 WHERE patient_id = 1; -- display the patient we just updated SELECT * FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 1;

blocks.html: It is the WHERE clause that determines how many records will be updated.
The following SQL statement will update the allergies to 'NKA' (no known allergies) for all records where allergies is NULL

blocks.text: UPDATE patients SET allergies = 'NKA' WHERE allergies IS NULL; -- display the patients table SELECT * FROM patients;

blocks.html: The WHERE clause is used to filter records.
It is used to extract only those records that fulfill a specified condition.

blocks.text: SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM tablename WHERE condition;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all the patients with the gender "F", in the "patients" table:
SQL requires single quotes around text values (most database systems will also allow double quotes).
However, numeric fields should not be enclosed in quotes:
The following operators can be used in the WHERE clause:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE patient_id <> 5; -- No patient_id 5 row
SELECT * FROM patients WHERE patient_id BETWEEN 4 AND 6;
SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name LIKE 'a%'; -- First names starting with 'a'. -- View sql patterns for more info.
SELECT * FROM patients WHERE patient_id IN (1, 3, 6, 9); -- the values can be replaced with a sub-query.
SQL AND, OR and NOT Operators

blocks.html: The WHERE clause can be combined with AND, OR, and NOT operators.
The AND and OR operators are used to filter records based on more than one condition:
- The AND operator displays a record if all the conditions separated by AND are TRUE.
- The OR operator displays a record if any of the conditions separated by OR is TRUE.
The NOT operator displays a record if the condition(s) is NOT TRUE.

blocks.text: SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name WHERE condition1 AND condition2 AND condition3 ...;
SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name WHERE condition1 OR condition2 OR condition3 ...;
SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name WHERE NOT condition;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all fields from "patients" where first_name is "John" AND city is "Toronto":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name = 'John' AND city = 'Toronto';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all fields from "patients" where city is "Hamilton" OR "Toronto":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE city = 'Hamilton' OR city = 'Toronto';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all fields from "patients" where province_id is NOT "ON" (Ontario):

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE NOT province_id = 'ON';

blocks.html: The ORDER BY keyword is used to sort the result-set in ascending or descending order.
The ORDER BY keyword sorts the records in ascending order by default. To sort the records in descending order, use the DESC keyword.

blocks.text: SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name ORDER BY column1, column2, ... ASC|DESC;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients from the "patients" table, sorted by the "first_name" column:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY first_name;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients from the "patients" table, sorted DESCENDING by the "first_name" column:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY first_name DESC;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients from the "patients" table, sorted by the "first_name" and the "last_name" column. This means that it orders by first_name, but if some rows have the same first_name, it orders them by last_name:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY first_name, last_name;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients from the "patients" table, sorted ascending by the "first_name" and descending by the "last_name" column:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY first_name ASC, last_name DESC;

blocks.html: The LIKE operator is used in a WHERE clause to search for a specified pattern in a column.
There are two wildcards often used in conjunction with the LIKE operator:
- The percent sign (%) represents zero, one, or multiple characters
- The underscore sign (_) represents one, single character
The percent sign and the underscore can also be used in combinations

blocks.text: SELECT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name WHERE column LIKE pattern;

-- Finds any values that start with "a" WHERE first_name LIKE 'a%'; -- Finds any values that end with "a" WHERE first_name LIKE '%a'; -- Finds any values that have "or" in any position WHERE first_name LIKE '%or%'; -- Finds any values that have "r" in the second position WHERE first_name LIKE '_r%'; -- Finds any values that start with "a" and are at least 2 characters WHERE first_name LIKE 'a_%'; -- Finds any values that start with "a" and are at least 3 characters WHERE first_name LIKE 'a__%'; -- Finds any values that start with "a" and ends with "o" WHERE first_name LIKE 'a%o';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a first_name starting with "a":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name LIKE 'a%';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a first_name ending with "a":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name LIKE '%a';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a first_name that have "or" in any position:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name LIKE '%or%';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a first_name that have "r" in the second position:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name LIKE '_r%';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a first_name that starts with "a" and are at least 3 characters in length:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name LIKE 'a__%';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a first_name that starts with "a" and ends with "o":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name LIKE 'a%o';

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a first_name that does NOT start with "a":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name NOT LIKE 'a%';

blocks.html: The IN operator allows you to specify multiple values in a WHERE clause.
The IN operator is a shorthand for multiple OR conditions.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE column_name IN (value1, value2, ...);

blocks.html: or:

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE column_name IN (SELECT STATEMENT);

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients that are located in "SK", "AB" or "MB":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE province_id IN ('SK', 'AB', 'MB');

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients that are NOT located in "SK", "AB" or "MB":

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE province_id NOT IN ('SK', 'AB', 'MB');

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients that have the same first_name as a doctor:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name IN (SELECT first_name FROM doctors); -- Try running just the sub query to see the list

blocks.html: The BETWEEN operator selects values within a given range. The values can be numbers, text, or dates.
The BETWEEN operator is inclusive: begin and end values are included.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE column_name BETWEEN value1 AND value2;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a weight between 100 and 120:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE weight BETWEEN 100 AND 120;

blocks.html: To display the products outside the range of the previous example, use NOT BETWEEN:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE weight NOT BETWEEN 100 AND 120;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all patients with a weight between 100 and 120. In addition; do not show patients located in 'ON', 'SK', or 'AB':

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE weight BETWEEN 100 AND 120 AND province_id NOT IN ('ON', 'SK', 'AB');

blocks.html: Text is compared based on the ASCII value of the text. For example, 'c'(99) is between 'a'(97) and 'e'(101) but 'C'(67) is not between 'a'(97) and 'e'(101).
The following SQL statement selects all patients with their first_name between 'Alex' and 'Ben':

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE first_name BETWEEN 'Alex' AND 'Ben';

blocks.html: A JOIN clause is used to combine rows from two or more tables, based on a related column (primary, foreign key) between them.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table1 JOIN table2 ON table1.column_name = table2.column_name;

blocks.html: Let's look at a selection from the "unit_dose_orders" (outdated) table:
Then, look at a selection from the "patients" table:

blocks.text: patient_id | first_name | last_name 1 | Miyuki | Riviera 2 | Deunan | Knute 3 | Lois | McAllister

blocks.html: Notice that the "patient_id" column in the "unit_dose_orders" table refers to the "patient_id" in the "patients" table. The relationship between the two tables is the "patient_id" column.
The following SQL statement selects records that have matching values in both tables:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients p JOIN admissions a ON a.patient_id = p.patient_id;

blocks.html: It is rare to need a join other than (INNER) JOIN.
DISCLAIMER: Our tool only supports INNER/LEFT JOIN
Here are the different types of the JOINs in SQL:
- (INNER) JOIN: Returns records that have matching values in both tables
- LEFT (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all records from the left table, and the matched records from the right table
- RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all records from the right table, and the matched records from the left table
- FULL (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all records when there is a match in either left or right table

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients p JOIN admissions a ON a.patient_id = p.patient_id JOIN doctors ph ON ph.doctor_id = a.attending_doctor_id;

blocks.html: The UNION operator is used to combine the result-set of two or more SELECT statements.
- Every SELECT statement within UNION must have the same number of columns
- The columns must also have similar data types
- The columns in every SELECT statement must also be in the same order

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table1 UNION SELECT column_name(s) FROM table2;

blocks.html: The UNION operator selects only distinct values by default. To allow duplicate values, use UNION ALL:

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table1 UNION ALL SELECT column_name(s) FROM table2;

blocks.html: Note: The column names in the result-set are usually equal to the column names in the first SELECT statement.
The following SQL statement returns the first_names (only distinct values) from both the "patients" and the "doctors" table:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name FROM patients UNION SELECT first_name FROM doctors ORDER BY first_name;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement returns the first_names (duplicate values also) from both the "patients" and the "doctors" table:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name FROM patients UNION ALL SELECT first_name FROM doctors ORDER BY first_name;

blocks.html: The GROUP BY statement groups rows that have the same values into summary rows, like "find the number of patients in each province".
The GROUP BY statement is often used with aggregate functions (COUNT(), MAX(), MIN(), SUM(), AVG()) to group the result-set by one or more columns.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE condition GROUP BY column_name(s);

blocks.html: The following SQL statement lists the number of patients in each province:

blocks.text: SELECT COUNT(*), province_id FROM patients GROUP BY province_id;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement lists the number of patients in each province, sorted high to low:

blocks.text: SELECT COUNT(*), province_id FROM patients GROUP BY province_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;

blocks.html: The HAVING clause was added to SQL because the WHERE keyword cannot be used with aggregate functions.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE condition GROUP BY column_name(s) HAVING condition ORDER BY column_name(s);

blocks.html: The following SQL statement lists the names of patients with a common first_name (> 30 occurrences):

blocks.text: SELECT COUNT(*), first_name FROM patients GROUP BY first_name HAVING COUNT(*) > 30;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement lists the names of patients with a common first_name (> 30 occurrences), sorted high to low:

blocks.text: SELECT COUNT(*), first_name FROM patients GROUP BY first_name HAVING COUNT(*) > 30 ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;

blocks.html: The CASE statement goes through conditions and returns a value when the first condition is met (like an if-then-else statement). Once a condition is true, it will stop reading and return the result. If no conditions are true, it returns the value in the ELSE clause.
If there is no ELSE part and no conditions are true, it returns NULL.

blocks.text: CASE WHEN condition1 THEN result1 WHEN condition2 THEN result2 WHEN conditionN THEN resultN ELSE result END;

blocks.html: The following SQL goes through conditions and returns a value when the first condition is met:

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, height, CASE WHEN height > 175 THEN 'height is greater than 175' WHEN height = 175 THEN 'height is 175' ELSE 'height is under 175' END AS height_group FROM patients;

blocks.html: The following SQL will order the patients by allergies. However, if allergies is NULL, then order by patient_id:

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, first_name, allergies FROM patients ORDER BY (CASE WHEN allergies IS NULL THEN first_name ELSE allergies END);

blocks.html: The SELECT DISTINCT statement is used to return only distinct (different) values.
Inside a table, a column often contains many duplicate values; and sometimes you only want to list the different (distinct) values.

blocks.text: SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2, ... FROM table_name;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement selects all (including duplicates) values from the first_name column in the patients table:
Now, let us use the SELECT DISTINCT statement and see the result:
The following SQL statement lists the number of different (distinct) first_name values:
The EXISTS operator is used to test for the existence of any record in a subquery.
The EXISTS operator returns TRUE if the subquery returns one or more records.

Note: SQL statements that use the EXISTS condition are very inefficient since the sub-query is rerun for EVERY row in the outer query's table. There are more efficient ways to write most queries, that do not use the EXISTS condition.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE EXISTS (SELECT column_name FROM table_name WHERE condition);

blocks.html: The following SQL statement returns all patients who were diagnosed with pregnancy:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE EXISTS (SELECT diagnosis FROM admissions WHERE patients.patient_id = admissions.patient_id AND diagnosis = 'Pregnancy');

blocks.html: The above SQL statement can be written more efficiently as:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients JOIN admissions ON patients.patient_id = admissions.patient_id WHERE diagnosis = 'Pregnancy';

blocks.html: The ANY and ALL operators allow you to perform a comparison between a single column value and a range of other values.
DISCLAIMER: This tool does not support the Any/All Operator.
The ANY operator:

items: returns a boolean value as a result
returns TRUE if ANY of the subquery values meet the condition

blocks.html: ANY means that the condition will be true if the operation is true for any of the values in the range.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE column_name operator ANY (SELECT column_name FROM table_name WHERE condition);

blocks.html: The ALL operator:

items: returns a boolean value as a result
returns TRUE if ALL of the subquery values meet the condition
is used with SELECT, WHERE and HAVING statements

blocks.html: ALL means that the condition will be true only if the operation is true for all values in the range.

blocks.text: SELECT ALL column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE condition;
ALL Syntax With WHERE or HAVING
SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name WHERE column_name operator ALL (SELECT column_name FROM table_name WHERE condition);
SQL IFNULL(), ISNULL(), COALESCE(), and NVL() Functions

blocks.html: The IFNULL function goes by many names depending on what SQL dialect you are using. We use IFNULL but your specific language may use ISNULL, COALESCE, or NVL — most function the same.
The allergies column displays NULL for some rows. We want it to display a default value instead.
The IFNULL() function returns an alternative value if an expression is NULL:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, IFNULL(allergies,'none') AS allergies FROM patients;

blocks.html: Or using COALESCE():

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, COALESCE(allergies,'none') AS allergies FROM patients;

blocks.html: The ISNULL() function returns an alternative value if the expression is NULL:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, ISNULL(allergies,'none') AS allergies FROM patients;

blocks.html: The IsNull() function returns TRUE (1) if the expression is NULL, otherwise FALSE (0):

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, IIF(ISNULL(allergies,0),allergies) AS allergies FROM patients;

blocks.html: The NVL() function achieves the same result:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, NVL(allergies,'none') AS allergies FROM patients;

blocks.html: A field with a NULL value is a field with no value.
If a field in a table is optional, it is possible to insert a new record or update a record without adding a value to this field. Then, the field will be saved with a NULL value.

blocks.text: How to Test for NULL Values?

blocks.html: It is not possible to test for NULL values with comparison operators, such as =, <, or <>.
We have to use the IS NULL and IS NOT NULL operators instead.

blocks.text: SELECT column_names FROM table_name WHERE column_name IS NULL;
SELECT column_names FROM table_name WHERE column_name IS NOT NULL;

blocks.html: The IS NULL operator is used to test for empty values (NULL values).
The following SQL lists all patients with a NULL value in the "allergies" field:

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients WHERE allergies IS NULL;

blocks.html: SQL aliases are used to give a table, or a column in a table, a temporary name. Aliases are often used to make column names more readable.
An alias only exists for the duration of that query. An alias is created with the AS keyword. Depending on the SQL dialect, the AS keyword may be optional.

blocks.text: SELECT column_name AS alias_name FROM table_name;
SELECT column_name(s) FROM table_name AS alias_name;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement creates two aliases, one for the weight column and one for the height column:

blocks.text: SELECT avg(weight) AS average_weight, avg(height) AS average_height FROM patients;

blocks.html: The following SQL renames the admissions table as 'a' and the patients table as 'p':

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM patients AS p JOIN admissions AS a ON a.patient_id = p.patient_id;

blocks.html: The COUNT() function returns the number of rows that match a specified criterion.
COUNT() usually has * as its parameter because the name of the column does not usually matter since they all have the same count.

blocks.text: SELECT COUNT(column_name) FROM table_name WHERE condition;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement finds the number of patients that weigh over 120Kg:

blocks.text: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM patients WHERE weight > 120;

blocks.html: The AVG() function returns the average value of a numeric column.

blocks.text: SELECT AVG(column_name) FROM table_name WHERE condition;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement finds the average weight of patients:
The SUM() function returns the total sum of a numeric column.

blocks.text: SELECT SUM(column_name) FROM table_name WHERE condition;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement finds the sum of patients' weight:
The MAX() function returns the largest value of the selected column.

blocks.text: SELECT MAX(column_name) FROM table_name WHERE condition;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement finds the highest patient's weight:
The MIN() function returns the smallest value of the selected column.

blocks.text: SELECT MIN(column_name) FROM table_name WHERE condition;

blocks.html: The following SQL statement finds the lowest patient's weight:
Introduction to SQL Window Functions
The aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX, etc) perform calculations across a set of rows and return a single output row.
The following query uses the AVG() aggregate function to calculate the average weight of all patients:

blocks.text: SELECT AVG(weight) as avg_weight FROM patients;

blocks.html: As shown, all rows are grouped into a single row. A window function does not group rows into a single row.
Using AVG() as a window function:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, last_name, weight, AVG(weight) OVER() as avg_weight FROM patients;

blocks.html: The OVER() clause signals that AVG() is used as a window function.

blocks.text: window_function_name ( expression ) OVER ( partition_clause order_clause frame_clause )

blocks.html: Clauses explanation:

items: window_function_name: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), SUM(), AVG(), etc.
expression: the target column or expression.
OVER clause: defines partitions and order of rows.
partition_clause: divides rows into partitions. Syntax: PARTITION BY expr1, expr2, ...
order_clause: orders rows in a partition. Syntax: ORDER BY expression [ASC|DESC] [NULL {FIRST|LAST}], ...
frame_clause: subset of the partition. Syntax: {ROWS|RANGE} frame_start [{BETWEEN frame_start AND frame_end}]

blocks.html: Frame options:

items: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING: starts at first row of partition
N PRECEDING: starts N rows before current row
CURRENT ROW: current row
UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING: ends at last row
N FOLLOWING: ends N rows after current row

blocks.html: Window function types:

items: Value window functions: FIRST_VALUE(), LAST_VALUE(), LAG(), LEAD()
Ranking window functions: CUME_DIST(), DENSE_RANK(), NTILE(), PERCENT_RANK(), RANK(), ROW_NUMBER()
Aggregate window functions: AVG(), COUNT(), MAX(), MIN(), SUM()

blocks.html: The result of a window function cannot be filtered by WHERE or HAVING. Use a WITH clause to create a temporary table.
Rolling sum example:

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, first_name, weight, sum(weight) over(order by patient_id) as rolling_sum FROM patients;

blocks.html: Incorrect filtering (does not work):

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, first_name, weight, sum(weight) over(order by patient_id) as rolling_sum FROM patients WHERE rolling_sum < 1000;

blocks.html: Correct filtering using WITH:

blocks.text: WITH rolling_sum_table AS ( SELECT patient_id, first_name, weight, sum(weight) over(order by patient_id) as rolling_sum FROM patients ) SELECT * FROM rolling_sum_table WHERE rolling_sum < 1000;

blocks.html: The LAG() function returns the record offset by the specified amount.

items: expression: Required. The value to be returned based on the specified offset. Must be a scalar value; cannot be an analytic function.
offset: Optional. Number of rows back from the current row. Default is 1. Must be positive; cannot be negative or an analytic function.

blocks.html: The following SQL statement displays each patient's first_name along with the first_name of the previous patient:

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, first_name, LAG(first_name, 1) OVER() AS previous_name FROM patients;

blocks.html: The LEAD() function returns the record offset by the specified amount forward.

items: expression: Required. The value to be returned based on the specified offset. Must be a scalar value; cannot be an analytic function.
offset: Optional. Number of rows forward from the current row. Default is 1. Must be positive; cannot be negative or an analytic function.

blocks.html: The following SQL statement displays each patient's first_name along with the first_name of the next patient:

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, first_name, LEAD(first_name, 1) OVER() AS next_name FROM patients;

blocks.html: The FIRST_VALUE() function is a window function that returns the first value in an ordered partition of a result set.

blocks.text: FIRST_VALUE ( scalar_expression ) OVER ( [PARTITION BY partition_expression, ... ] ORDER BY sort_expression [ASC | DESC], ... )

items: scalar_expression: Required. An expression evaluated against the value of the first row in an ordered partition. Can be a column, subquery, or expression that evaluates to a single value. Cannot be a window function.

blocks.html: The following SQL statement displays the oldest patient's birth_date for the province the patient is in:

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, province_id, FIRST_VALUE(birth_date) OVER( PARTITION BY province_id -- group by province_id ORDER BY birth_date -- order by birth_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS oldest_birth_date FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;

blocks.html: The LAST_VALUE() function is a window function that returns the last value in an ordered partition of a result set.

blocks.text: LAST_VALUE ( scalar_expression ) OVER ( [PARTITION BY partition_expression, ... ] ORDER BY sort_expression [ASC | DESC], ... )

items: scalar_expression: Required. An expression evaluated against the value of the last row in an ordered partition. Can be a column, subquery, or expression that evaluates to a single value. Cannot be a window function.

blocks.html: The following SQL statement displays the youngest patient's birth_date for the province the patient is in:

blocks.text: SELECT patient_id, province_id, LAST_VALUE(birth_date) OVER( PARTITION BY province_id -- group by province_id ORDER BY birth_date -- order by birth_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS youngest_birth_date FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;

blocks.html: The CONCAT() function adds two or more expressions together.
Note: Depending on the SQL language, there may be built-in syntax for concatenation such as + or ||.

items: expression1, expression2, expression3, etc.: Required. The expressions to add together. If any expression is NULL, the result will be NULL.

blocks.html: The following SQL statement concatenates the first_name and last_name of each patient:

blocks.text: SELECT CONCAT(first_name,' ', last_name) AS full_name FROM patients;

blocks.html: The LEN() function returns the length of a string in bytes.
Note: Depending on the SQL language, LEN() may also be called LENGTH().

items: string: Required. The string to calculate the length for.

blocks.html: The following SQL statement shows each patient's first_name and the length of that name:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, LEN(first_name) AS length_of_name FROM patients;

blocks.html: The UPPER() function returns a string in uppercase. Example: 'ExAmple' → 'EXAMPLE'.
Note: Depending on the SQL language, UPPER() may also be called UCASE().

items: string: Required. The string to convert to uppercase.

blocks.html: The following SQL statement shows each patient's first_name in uppercase:

blocks.text: SELECT first_name, UPPER(first_name) AS uppercase_name FROM patients;

blocks.html: The LOWER() function returns a string in lowercase. Example: 'ExAmple' → 'example'.
Note: Depending on the SQL language, LOWER() may also be called LCASE().

items: string: Required. The string to convert to lowercase.

blocks.text: SQL Data Types for MySQL, SQL Server, and MS Access

blocks.html: The data type of a column defines what value the column can hold: integer, character, money, date and time, binary, and more.
Each column in a table requires a name and a data type. The SQL developer chooses the type of data stored, which affects storage, validation, and behavior. Note: data types differ across databases.

items: CHAR(size): Fixed length string, 0-255 characters.
VARCHAR(size): Variable length string, up to 65535 characters.
BINARY(size): Fixed-length binary string.
VARBINARY(size): Variable-length binary string.
TINYBLOB / TINYTEXT: Max length 255 bytes / chars.
TEXT / BLOB: Max length 65535 bytes / chars.
MEDIUMTEXT / MEDIUMBLOB: Max length 16,777,215 bytes / chars.
LONGTEXT / LONGBLOB: Max length 4,294,967,295 bytes / chars.
ENUM / SET: Predefined lists of values.
INT / INTEGER / BIGINT / SMALLINT / MEDIUMINT / TINYINT: Integer types with various ranges.
FLOAT / DOUBLE / DECIMAL: Floating-point and exact numeric types.
BIT: Bit values, 1–64 bits.
BOOL / BOOLEAN: True/False values.
DATE: YYYY-MM-DD
DATETIME / TIMESTAMP: Date and time values
TIME: Time only
YEAR: Four-digit year
String: char(n), varchar(n), varchar(max), text, nchar, nvarchar(n), nvarchar(max), ntext
Numeric: bit, tinyint, smallint, int, bigint, decimal(p,s), numeric(p,s), smallmoney, money, float(n), real
Date/Time: datetime, datetime2, smalldatetime, date, time, datetimeoffset, timestamp
Other: sql_variant, uniqueidentifier, xml, cursor, table
Text, Memo, Byte, Integer, Long, Single, Double, Currency, AutoNumber, Date/Time, Yes/No, Ole Object, Hyperlink, Lookup Wizard

blocks.html: The CREATE TABLE statement is used to create a new table in a database.

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE table_name ( column1 datatype, column2 datatype, column3 datatype, ... );

blocks.html: The column parameters specify the names of the columns, and the datatype parameter specifies the type of data the column can hold (e.g., varchar, integer, date).
Create a table called Persons with 5 columns:

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE Persons ( PersonID int, LastName varchar(255), FirstName varchar(255), Address varchar(255), City varchar(255) );

blocks.html: You can create a new table as a copy of an existing table. All or specific columns can be selected:

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE new_table_name AS SELECT column1, column2,... FROM existing_table_name WHERE ...;

blocks.html: Example: Copy selected columns from the patients table:

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE TestPatients AS SELECT patient_id, first_name, last_name FROM patients; -- Verify the new table SELECT * FROM TestPatients;

blocks.html: The DROP TABLE statement is used to remove an existing table from a database.
Note: Be careful before dropping a table. Deleting a table will result in the loss of all data stored in it!
The following SQL statement drops the existing table patients:

blocks.text: DROP TABLE patients; -- Attempt to query the table after dropping it SELECT * FROM patients;

blocks.html: The ALTER TABLE statement is used to add, delete, or modify columns in an existing table. It is also used to add or drop various constraints on an existing table.
Note: ALTER/MODIFY COLUMN syntax is not supported in this tutorial.

blocks.text: ALTER TABLE table_name ADD column_name datatype;

blocks.html: Example: Add an "email" column to the "patients" table:

blocks.text: ALTER TABLE patients ADD email varchar(255); SELECT patient_id, email FROM patients;

blocks.html: To delete a column in a table:

blocks.text: ALTER TABLE table_name DROP COLUMN column_name;

blocks.html: Example: Delete the "last_name" column from the "patients" table:

blocks.text: ALTER TABLE patients DROP COLUMN last_name; SELECT * FROM patients;

blocks.html: To change the data type of a column in a table:

blocks.text: -- SQL Server / MS Access ALTER TABLE table_name ALTER COLUMN column_name datatype; -- MySQL / Oracle (prior to 10G) ALTER TABLE table_name MODIFY COLUMN column_name datatype; -- Oracle 10G and later ALTER TABLE table_name MODIFY column_name datatype;

blocks.html: SQL constraints are used to specify rules for data in a table.
Constraints can be specified when the table is created with the CREATE TABLE statement, or after the table is created with the ALTER TABLE statement.

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE table_name ( column1 datatype constraint, column2 datatype constraint, column3 datatype constraint, .... );

blocks.html: Constraints are used to limit the type of data that can go into a table. This ensures the accuracy and reliability of the data. If a constraint is violated, the action is aborted.
Constraints can be column level (applies to a single column) or table level (applies to the whole table).

items: NOT NULL - Ensures that a column cannot have a NULL value
UNIQUE - Ensures that all values in a column are different
PRIMARY KEY - A combination of NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Uniquely identifies each row in a table
FOREIGN KEY - Prevents actions that would destroy links between tables
CHECK - Ensures that the values in a column satisfy a specific condition
DEFAULT - Sets a default value for a column if no value is specified

blocks.html: By default, a column can hold NULL values.
The NOT NULL constraint enforces a column to NOT accept NULL values.
This ensures a field always contains a value, which means you cannot insert a new record or update a record without providing a value for this field.
The following SQL ensures that the "ID", "LastName", and "FirstName" columns will NOT accept NULL values when creating the "Persons" table:

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255) NOT NULL, Age int );

blocks.html: Note: We do not support this syntax directly.
To create a NOT NULL constraint on the "Age" column after the table is already created:

blocks.text: ALTER TABLE Persons MODIFY Age int NOT NULL;

blocks.html: The UNIQUE constraint ensures that all values in a column are different.
Both the UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints provide a guarantee for uniqueness for a column or set of columns. A PRIMARY KEY constraint automatically has a UNIQUE constraint.
You can have many UNIQUE constraints per table, but only one PRIMARY KEY constraint per table.
The following SQL creates a UNIQUE constraint on the "ID" column when the "Persons" table is created:

blocks.text: -- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL UNIQUE, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int ); -- display the empty table Persons SELECT * FROM Persons;

blocks.html: MySQL alternative syntax:

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, UNIQUE (ID) );

blocks.html: To name a UNIQUE constraint or define it on multiple columns:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, CONSTRAINT UC_Person UNIQUE (ID, LastName) );

blocks.html: To create a UNIQUE constraint on the "ID" column after the table is already created:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons ADD UNIQUE (ID); -- Naming or multiple columns ALTER TABLE Persons ADD CONSTRAINT UC_Person UNIQUE (ID, LastName);

blocks.html: To drop a UNIQUE constraint:

blocks.text: -- MySQL ALTER TABLE Persons DROP INDEX UC_Person; -- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons DROP CONSTRAINT UC_Person;

blocks.html: The PRIMARY KEY constraint uniquely identifies each record in a table.
Primary keys must contain UNIQUE values, and cannot contain NULL values.
A table can have only ONE primary key; this primary key can consist of single or multiple columns (fields).
The following SQL creates a PRIMARY KEY on the "ID" column when the "Persons" table is created:

blocks.text: -- MySQL CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, PRIMARY KEY (ID) );
-- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int );

blocks.html: To name a PRIMARY KEY constraint or define it on multiple columns:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, CONSTRAINT PK_Person PRIMARY KEY (ID, LastName) );

blocks.html: To create a PRIMARY KEY on an existing table:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons ADD PRIMARY KEY (ID); -- Naming or multiple columns ALTER TABLE Persons ADD CONSTRAINT PK_Person PRIMARY KEY (ID, LastName);

blocks.html: Note: If you use ALTER TABLE to add a primary key, the primary key column(s) must have been declared NOT NULL when the table was first created.

blocks.text: -- MySQL ALTER TABLE Persons DROP PRIMARY KEY; -- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons DROP CONSTRAINT PK_Person;

blocks.html: The FOREIGN KEY constraint is used to prevent actions that would destroy links between tables.
A FOREIGN KEY is a field (or collection of fields) in one table that refers to the PRIMARY KEY in another table.
The table with the foreign key is called the child table, and the table with the primary key is called the referenced or parent table.
The FOREIGN KEY constraint prevents invalid data from being inserted into the foreign key column because it must exist in the parent table.
The following SQL creates a FOREIGN KEY on the "PersonID" column when the "Orders" table is created:

blocks.text: -- MySQL CREATE TABLE Orders ( OrderID int NOT NULL, OrderNumber int NOT NULL, PersonID int, PRIMARY KEY (OrderID), FOREIGN KEY (PersonID) REFERENCES Persons(PersonID) );
-- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Orders ( OrderID int NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, OrderNumber int NOT NULL, PersonID int FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Persons(PersonID) );

blocks.html: To name a FOREIGN KEY constraint or define it on multiple columns:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Orders ( OrderID int NOT NULL, OrderNumber int NOT NULL, PersonID int, PRIMARY KEY (OrderID), CONSTRAINT FK_PersonOrder FOREIGN KEY (PersonID) REFERENCES Persons(PersonID) );

blocks.html: To create a FOREIGN KEY on an existing table:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Orders ADD FOREIGN KEY (PersonID) REFERENCES Persons(PersonID); -- Naming or multiple columns ALTER TABLE Orders ADD CONSTRAINT FK_PersonOrder FOREIGN KEY (PersonID) REFERENCES Persons(PersonID);
-- MySQL ALTER TABLE Orders DROP FOREIGN KEY FK_PersonOrder; -- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Orders DROP CONSTRAINT FK_PersonOrder;

blocks.html: The CHECK constraint is used to limit the value range that can be placed in a column.
If you define a CHECK constraint on a column, it will allow only certain values for that column.
If you define a CHECK constraint on a table, it can limit values in certain columns based on values in other columns in the same row.
The following SQL creates a CHECK constraint on the "Age" column when the "Persons" table is created. The CHECK constraint ensures that the age of a person must be 18 or older:

blocks.text: -- MySQL CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, CHECK (Age>=18) );
-- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int CHECK (Age>=18) );

blocks.html: To allow naming of a CHECK constraint or defining it on multiple columns:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, City varchar(255), CONSTRAINT CHK_Person CHECK (Age>=18 AND City='Sandnes') );

blocks.html: To create a CHECK constraint on an existing table:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons ADD CHECK (Age>=18); -- Naming or multiple columns ALTER TABLE Persons ADD CONSTRAINT CHK_PersonAge CHECK (Age>=18 AND City='Sandnes');
-- MySQL ALTER TABLE Persons DROP CHECK CHK_PersonAge; -- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons DROP CONSTRAINT CHK_PersonAge;

blocks.html: The DEFAULT constraint is used to set a default value for a column.
The default value will be added to all new records if no other value is specified.
Set a default value for the "City" column when creating the "Persons" table:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Persons ( ID int NOT NULL, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, City varchar(255) DEFAULT 'Sandnes' );

blocks.html: DEFAULT can also use system values like current_timestamp:

blocks.text: -- MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access CREATE TABLE Orders ( ID int NOT NULL, OrderNumber int NOT NULL, OrderDate date DEFAULT current_timestamp ); -- Example insert INSERT INTO Orders (ID, OrderNumber) VALUES (1,1); SELECT * FROM Orders;

blocks.html: Create a DEFAULT constraint on an existing column:

blocks.text: -- MySQL ALTER TABLE Persons ALTER City SET DEFAULT 'Sandnes'; -- SQL Server ALTER TABLE Persons ADD CONSTRAINT df_City DEFAULT 'Sandnes' FOR City; -- MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons ALTER COLUMN City SET DEFAULT 'Sandnes'; -- Oracle ALTER TABLE Persons MODIFY City DEFAULT 'Sandnes';
-- MySQL ALTER TABLE Persons ALTER City DROP DEFAULT; -- SQL Server / Oracle / MS Access ALTER TABLE Persons ALTER COLUMN City DROP DEFAULT;

blocks.html: Auto-increment allows a unique number to be generated automatically when a new record is inserted into a table. Often this is the primary key field that is created automatically for each new record.

blocks.text: CREATE TABLE Persons ( Personid int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int, PRIMARY KEY (Personid) ); -- Start AUTO_INCREMENT with another value ALTER TABLE Persons AUTO_INCREMENT=100; -- Insert without specifying Personid INSERT INTO Persons (FirstName, LastName) VALUES ('Lars','Monsen');

CREATE TABLE Persons ( Personid int IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int ); -- Tip: Start at 10, increment by 5 -- Personid int IDENTITY(10,5) PRIMARY KEY INSERT INTO Persons (FirstName, LastName) VALUES ('Lars','Monsen');

CREATE TABLE Persons ( Personid AUTOINCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL, FirstName varchar(255), Age int ); -- Tip: Start at 10, increment by 5 -- AUTOINCREMENT(10,5) INSERT INTO Persons (FirstName, LastName) VALUES ('Lars','Monsen');

blocks.html: Oracle requires a sequence object to implement auto-increment:

blocks.text: -- Create sequence CREATE SEQUENCE seq_person MINVALUE 1 START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1 CACHE 10; -- Insert using nextval INSERT INTO Persons (Personid, FirstName, LastName) VALUES (seq_person.nextval, 'Lars', 'Monsen');

blocks.html: The CREATE INDEX statement is used to create indexes in tables. Indexes help retrieve data from the database faster. Users cannot see the indexes—they are only used to speed up searches and queries.
Note: Updating a table with indexes takes more time than updating a table without, because indexes also need updating. Only create indexes on columns that will be frequently searched against.

blocks.text: -- Creates a regular index (duplicate values allowed) CREATE INDEX index_name ON table_name (column1, column2, ...); -- Creates a unique index (duplicate values not allowed) CREATE UNIQUE INDEX index_name ON table_name (column1, column2, ...);

blocks.html: Create an index named "idx_lastname" on the "last_name" column in the "patients" table:
Create an index on multiple columns (last_name + first_name):

blocks.text: CREATE INDEX idx_pname ON patients (last_name, first_name);

blocks.html: Use DROP INDEX to delete an index. Syntax varies by database:

blocks.text: -- MS Access DROP INDEX index_name ON table_name; -- SQL Server DROP INDEX table_name.index_name; -- DB2 / Oracle DROP INDEX index_name; -- MySQL ALTER TABLE table_name DROP INDEX index_name;
